hints: Look closely at lactide, it is a cyclic molecule with two ester groups, so think about which functional groups must join to make an ester.
Count the carbons in lactide and notice the two methyl side chains, each half of the ring must supply one methyl group and three carbons in total.
Imagine splitting the ring open at the two ester links and adding water back, the two identical fragments you get reveal the hydroxy acid monomer.
walkthrough:
**Spot the functional groups in lactide**

Lactide is a cyclic diester. It has two $-COO-$ ester linkages in a six-membered ring.

Esters are made from a carboxylic acid plus an alcohol:
$$\text{R-COOH + HO-R'} \rightarrow \text{R-COO-R' + H}_2\text{O}$$

**Work backwards by hydrolysis**

Heating with acid catalyst causes esterification with loss of water. So to find the starting material, do the reverse in your head and add water across each ester bond.

Splitting both esters gives two identical hydroxy acid molecules, each with both an $-OH$ and a $-COOH$ group.

**Count atoms to identify the monomer**

Lactide has 6 carbons in total, with 2 methyl branches. Divide by 2 for the two monomers.

Each monomer must have 3 carbons with 1 methyl branch: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)COOH}$. That is 2-hydroxypropanoic acid, also called lactic acid:
$$2\,\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)COOH} \rightarrow \text{lactide} + 2\,\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

options.A: Hydroxyethanoic acid is $\text{HOCH}_2\text{COOH}$. Two molecules would form a cyclic diester with no methyl side chains, often called glycolide, not lactide which clearly has two methyl groups.
options.B: 2-hydroxybutanoic acid is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)COOH}$. It has four carbons with an ethyl group. Its cyclic dimer would have ethyl side chains, not the methyl side chains seen in lactide.
options.C: 2-hydroxypropanoic acid is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)COOH}$. Two molecules can undergo intermolecular esterification, losing two water molecules, to close into the six-membered ring with two methyl groups. This exactly matches the lactide structure.
options.D: 3-hydroxypropanoic acid is $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$. It has no methyl branch and the $-OH$ is on the beta carbon, not the alpha carbon. It cannot give the branched methyl groups on the ring carbons next to the carbonyls seen in lactide.
